purpose: Determine whether the spectral signal contributes more than generic grouping under a fixed single-edge search protocol.

fixed_protocol.backend: full graph with CUDA predictor inference and gradients
fixed_protocol.initial_support: Saved class-supportive saliency, identical for all policies on each query and budget
fixed_protocol.tie_rule: Same canonical positive-weight undirected edges and stable score ordering for every partition policy

compute_scope: All policies share candidate regions and maximum per-step proposal counts. Actual evaluated proposal counts and search times are recorded and need not match. CPU union-find follows CPU sorting; diffusion filtering runs on CUDA, while the existing large-graph eigen control still uses CPU ARPACK. Timings are not a controlled end-to-end speedup study.
source_verification: All recorded source hashes matched current source after both runs completed.

observations.Cora: Every grouping policy ties ungrouped search on both binary metrics for all sixty query-budget pairs. Supports and continuous scores can differ.
observations.PubMed: The structural normalized-edge control ties ungrouped search on all sixty query-budget pairs. The eigen control and every diffusion/random seed each lose on one pair and tie on the other fifty-nine, with no binary wins.
observations.partition_shapes: Local candidate-group counts and cluster sizes differ substantially despite equal global cluster counts; these are recorded, not assumed matched.

shared_PubMed_loss.diagnostic_scope: Saved traces agree through the first accepted state and subsequently diverge for ungrouped versus diffusion-0. This is evidence of a search-trajectory difference, not an independently replayed causal attribution to a particular omitted proposal.

decision: Do not select a best-looking grouping seed or claim a spectral contribution from this pilot. Keep the optional signal alternative and all controls available, without changing the default method or manuscript numerical results.
limits: Two graphs and one model-training seed each, with previously used validation queries, do not establish general superiority or universal ineffectiveness.
Random grouping seeds are not independent training runs; budgets on the same query are dependent observations.
The eigen control retains the known repeated-eigenspace cutoff ambiguity and is not a unique reference embedding.
The common canonical tie rule differs from the legacy raw-edge ordering, so this benchmark isolates grouping policies internally rather than claiming bitwise replay of old partitions.
Binary ties do not imply equal continuous fidelity, explanations, or computation.
next_decision_gate: Assess the actual role of coarse groups in proposal coverage and computational cost before introducing more score variants. A stronger paper claim requires a reproducible benefit beyond ungrouped and nonspectral controls, not just a corrected spectral definition.
